items.answer: Presence is a subjective psychological state in which an experience generated by human-made technology is perceived as real, because the user fails to acknowledge the technology's role and perceives computer-generated stimuli as coming from the real world.
Frequency is a property of a sound wave, measured in hertz (Hz), that is the number of changes from one maximum to another maximum per second.
A sound wave is a plot of air pressure variation against time, in which pressure varies from one extreme to another like a sinusoidal wave.

Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.

Cybersickness (CS) is a condition primarily relevant to virtual reality that may be caused by multiple internal and external factors and in which a user may experience symptoms such as nausea, dizziness, headache, or disorientation.
Auditory sense is a human sense that responds to air pressure waves via mechanoreceptors in the ear.

questions.question: What do the social, warning, and primitive levels of sound perception produce together for a person?
options: an estimate of a sound source's location
an alignment of auditory and visual cues
an overall idea of the surroundings
an appraisal of a tone's perceived loudness
questions.explanation: The three levels of sound perception together give a person an overall idea of the surroundings. Sound location, loudness, and cue alignment are separate perceptual tasks, not the combined result of these three levels.

questions.question: Which statement describes warning-level sound perception?
options: It estimates the position of a sound source by hearing
It helps an individual carry out social interactions
It perceives background noises that are mostly ignored
It provides an alert about something, such as an event
questions.explanation: Warning-level sound perception provides an alert or warning about something, such as an event. Social interaction and ignored background noises belong to the social and primitive levels, while estimating position is sound localization.

questions.question: Why are stimuli that mainly produce primitive-level perception unsuitable when a VR system needs social-level perception?
options: They are cues that help a person with social interactions
They are signals used to estimate a sound's location
They are alerts that warn a person about a coming event
They are mostly ignored and may not guide action
questions.explanation: Primitive-level perception involves naive or background sounds that are mostly ignored and may not lead to meaningful action, so such stimuli would not support the intended social interaction. Cues for social interaction belong to the social level, not primitive-level perception.

data.text: Sound perception in XR is described at three levels: social, warning, and primitive. These levels separate sounds that support interaction, sounds that warn about events, and mostly ignored naive sounds. In XR design, identifying the intended level guides the developer in generating suitable auditory effects.
points: Sound perception has social, warning, and primitive levels that together give an overall idea of surroundings.
Social-level sound perception helps an individual carry out social interactions with other individuals.
Warning-level sound perception provides an alert or warning about something, such as an event.
Primitive-level sound perception is intuitive perception of mostly ignored naive sounds and may not lead to meaningful action.
Identifying the desired sound perception level helps developers generate suitable auditory effects for a virtual reality system.

questions.question: Compared with psychophysics, what is psychoacoustics?
options: A more general area that studies physical stimuli
An unrelated area that studies visual stimuli
A more specific area that studies sound stimuli
A narrower area that studies tactile stimuli
questions.explanation: Psychoacoustics is the more specific part of psychophysics concerned with perceptual phenomena produced by sound. It is not a more general, unrelated, or tactile-stimulus area.

questions.question: Under Weber's law, how is the just noticeable difference related to the magnitude of the stimulus?
options: It is proportional to the magnitude
It is constant for every magnitude
It is a fixed addition to the magnitude
It is inversely proportional to the magnitude
questions.explanation: Weber's law states delta M / M = C, so delta M = C M; the just noticeable difference therefore grows in proportion to stimulus magnitude rather than staying fixed or changing inversely.

questions.question: When the exponent in Stevens' power law is less than one, how does perceived magnitude behave as the physical stimulus magnitude grows?
options: It grows in exact proportion to the physical magnitude
It grows more slowly than the physical magnitude
It grows more quickly than the physical magnitude
It stays fixed while the physical magnitude grows
questions.explanation: Stevens' power law uses P = C M^x. When x is below one, an increase in physical magnitude produces a smaller relative increase in perceived magnitude. This is why a much higher pressure level for a 3000 Hz tone is perceived as only a bit louder.

questions.question: For a change in a stimulus to be perceived, where must the change be relative to the just noticeable difference?
options: Within the just noticeable difference
Above the just noticeable difference
Below the just noticeable difference
At the just noticeable difference
questions.explanation: A stimulus change is perceived when it is above the just noticeable difference. If the change is within or below the just noticeable difference, it is not perceived as changed.

data.text: Psychophysics provides the general study of how physical stimuli become perception, and psychoacoustics applies that study to sound. Its two main laws connect physical magnitude to perceived magnitude: Stevens' power law describes overall perceived loudness, while Weber's law and the just noticeable difference describe the smallest change a listener can detect. These principles apply to auditory perception, so changes must exceed the just noticeable difference to be perceived, and loudness exponents such as 0.67 show that large physical increases may produce only small perceived increases.
points: Psychophysics studies perceptual phenomena caused by physical stimuli; psychoacoustics is its sound-specific branch.
Stevens' power law relates perceived magnitude P to stimulus magnitude M by P = C M^x.
The just noticeable difference, noticed in at least 50% of trials, follows Weber's law: delta M / M = C.
Weber's law and Stevens' power law apply to auditory perception; a 3000 Hz pure tone's loudness exponent is 0.67.
A stimulus change is perceived only if it is above the just noticeable difference.

questions.question: Which physical property of a sound wave is called pitch?
options: The amplitude of a sound wave
The pressure variation of a sound wave
The wavelength of a sound wave
The frequency of a sound wave
questions.explanation: Pitch is the perceptual counterpart of a sound wave's frequency. Amplitude and pressure variation relate to strength or propagation of sound, while wavelength is a separate wave property.

questions.question: As sound frequency rises, what happens to the just noticeable difference needed to detect a frequency change?
options: It becomes a similar change in hertz and percentage
It becomes a larger change in hertz and percentage
It becomes a larger change in hertz but a smaller change in percentage
It becomes a smaller change in hertz and percentage
questions.explanation: The JND grows with frequency: from under 1 Hz at low frequencies to about 100 Hz at 10 kHz, and the required percentage also rises from 0.1% or less to at least 1%.

data.text: Pitch perception links the pitch of a sound to the frequency of its sound wave. The ability to notice a change in frequency depends on the frequency itself: the just noticeable difference grows as frequency rises, both in hertz and percentage. These perceptual principles guide auditory design in XR.
points: In pitch perception, the frequency of a sound wave is called pitch.
The just noticeable difference for sound frequency increases as frequency rises, from under 1 Hz to about 100 Hz.

questions.question: What can result from a mismatch between a sound's position and the corresponding visual object in virtual reality?
options: clear presence and reduced cybersickness
broken presence and cybersickness
steady tracking and reduced latency
fixed azimuth and stable elevation
questions.explanation: In virtual reality, matching auditory and visual cues helps the user place objects; when they disagree, presence can break down and cybersickness can appear. Mismatch does not improve presence, stabilize tracking, or fix coordinate values.

questions.question: What does the minimum audible angle measure?
options: the angle at the threshold of hearing for a source
the smallest detectable change in sound frequency
the shortest distance from the listener's head to a source
the smallest detectable angular change in source location
questions.explanation: The minimum audible angle applies the just noticeable difference idea to sound localization: it is the smallest angular variation in a sound source's position that a listener can detect. It is not a frequency difference, a distance, or a threshold-of-hearing angle.

questions.question: Which three quantities locate a sound source in the spherical coordinate system used for sound localization?
options: pitch, loudness, and duration
interaural time difference, interaural level difference, and head size
horizontal distance, vertical distance, and forward distance
azimuth, elevation, and radius
questions.explanation: The system uses azimuth in the horizontal plane, elevation relative to the horizontal plane, and radius as the distance from the listener's head. Pitch, loudness, duration, binaural cues, and simple Cartesian-like distances are not the named spherical-coordinate parameters.

questions.question: What two properties does the minimum audible angle depend on?
options: the listener's visual focus and head motion
the source's distance and loudness
the listener's head size and ear shape
the sound's frequency and direction
questions.explanation: The minimum audible angle varies with a sound's frequency and direction, so some frequency-direction combinations are easy to localize while others are hard. Distance, loudness, head anatomy, visual focus, and head motion are not the properties that determine its variation.

data.text: Sound localization is the psychoacoustic process by which a listener estimates where a sound source is. In VR, matching auditory and visual cues helps the user perceive object positions, while a mismatch can break presence and cause cybersickness. Spherical coordinates with azimuth, elevation, and radius specify source location, and minimum audible angle describes the smallest detectable angular change, which varies with frequency and direction.
points: Sound localization estimates the location of a sound source by hearing it.
In VR, sound localization matches auditory and visual cues to locate objects; mismatch can break presence and cause cybersickness.
Minimum audible angle (MAA) is the smallest detectable angular change, based on just noticeable difference, with the head as origin.
Spherical coordinates represent a sound source by azimuth (-180 to 180°), elevation (-90 to 90°), and radius from the head.
Minimum audible angle depends on sound frequency and direction; it can be 1 degree or extremely high.

questions.question: Which binaural sound-localization cue compares how strong the sound is at each ear?
options: Acoustic shadow
Interaural level difference
Interaural time difference
Head-related transfer function
questions.explanation: Interaural level difference is the binaural cue based on the difference in sound magnitude heard by each ear. Interaural time difference uses arrival-time differences, an acoustic shadow is a blocked wave, and an HRTF models the listener’s response rather than acting as a level cue.

questions.question: What happens in an acoustic shadow?
options: A sound wave fails to reach one ear due to obstruction or head position
A sound wave reaches one ear first due to obstruction or head position
A sound wave is reflected toward one ear due to obstruction or head position
A sound wave is delayed at both ears due to obstruction or head position
questions.explanation: An acoustic shadow occurs when part of a sound wave is kept from reaching one ear by an object in front of the source or by the head’s position. Reaching one ear first or being delayed at both ears describes timing effects, not an acoustic shadow.

questions.question: Why is an average-listener head-related transfer function often used in an XR system?
options: Each person’s HRTF is unique, so measuring every user’s HRTF is impractical
Each person’s HRTF depends on the XR display, so measuring every user’s HRTF is impractical
Each person’s HRTF is the same, so measuring every user’s HRTF is impractical
Each person’s HRTF depends on the room, so measuring every user’s HRTF is impractical
questions.explanation: HRTFs depend on the size and shape of the head, ears, and ear canal, so each person has a unique HRTF. Because individual measurement is impractical, systems use an average-listener HRTF.

questions.question: How can a pair of head-related transfer functions be used to render localized binaural sound?
options: By using them to measure the listener’s position in the scene
By using them to generate the images shown to the two eyes
By using them to generate the signals sent to the two ears
By using them to set a single loudness level for one ear
questions.explanation: A pair of HRTFs can synthesize binaural sound by shaping what each ear receives, which creates the perception that sound comes from a particular location. HRTFs are not used to generate visual images, and a single ear loudness level does not provide the two-ear pattern needed for binaural localization.

data.text: Sound localization cues can use one ear or both ears. Binaural cues compare the level and arrival time of sound at the ears, with acoustic shadowing affecting the level difference. In XR, the audio should move with the user and depend on listener actions. Head-related transfer functions model personal sound reception, but because individual HRTFs are impractical, systems use an average HRTF pair to synthesize localized binaural sound.
points: Sound localization cues are either monaural, involving one ear, or binaural, involving both ears.
Interaural level difference is the magnitude difference between ears, from an acoustic shadow, and can indicate direction.
Interaural time difference is the small arrival-time gap between the ears, used to locate a sound source.
An XR system's auditory component should be non-stationary, move with the user, and depend on listener actions.
HRTFs model personal sound reception, but systems use average HRTF pairs to synthesize localized binaural XR sound.

questions.question: Why can a mismatch between auditory and visual cues about a sound source's position break presence and lead to cybersickness in virtual reality?
questions.reference_answer: A mismatch can break presence because presence is the state in which the user cannot distinguish computer-generated stimuli from real-world stimuli, and in virtual reality sound localization uses matching auditory and visual cues. Sound localization estimates a sound source's location, and this matching helps the user perceive object positions relative to the user. The same mismatch can also cause cybersickness.

questions.question: How do interaural level difference and interaural time difference provide binaural cues for estimating the direction of a sound source?
questions.reference_answer: They are binaural sound localization cues. Interaural level difference is the difference in sound magnitude heard by each ear, with the unobstructed ear receiving stronger sound when an acoustic shadow occurs. Interaural time difference comes from the sound reaching one ear before the other because the ears are about 21.5 centimeters apart and sound travels that distance in about 0.6 milliseconds. The level and timing differences can indicate the direction from which the sound is coming.

questions.question: How does an average head-related transfer function allow an extended reality system to create a binaural localization effect despite each person's head-related transfer function being unique?
questions.reference_answer: An average listener's head-related transfer function can be used because individual users' HRTFs are impractical to determine when building a system, and HRTFs depend on a person's head, ears, and ear canal. A pair of HRTFs for both ears can synthesize binaural sound. By generating sound effects or placing sound receivers according to this model, a localization effect can be implemented in an extended reality system.

questions.question: Why is a change in the frequency of a low-frequency sound easier to perceive than the same percentage change at a high frequency?
questions.reference_answer: Pitch is the frequency of a sound wave, and a change must be above the just noticeable difference to be perceived. For sound frequency, the just noticeable difference increases as frequency increases: below 1000 Hz, a change of less than 1 Hz can be detected, while at 10,000 Hz it is about 100 Hz. In percentage terms, low frequencies can allow detection of 0.1% or less, whereas higher frequencies require at least 1%.
